Eucalyptus. A genus of trees native to Australia that dominates the continent's landscape and ecology. Over six hundred species of eucalyptus—ranging from shrubs to giants over three hundred feet tall—are uniquely adapted to Australia's arid, fire-prone climate through waxy leaves, deep root systems, and the ability to resprout after fire. The trees are so emblematic of Australia that they appear in its national symbolism, yet their introduction to other continents has sometimes proven ecologically invasive.

Leaves contain aromatic oils. The genus name derives from the Greek for "well-hidden," referring to the flower's hidden stamens, not the leaves' scent. Eucalyptus are perfectly adapted to drought and fire. Leaves have reduced surface area and waxy coating to minimize water loss. Many species release seeds only after fires, regenerating in the ash.

The koala is almost exclusively dependent on eucalyptus leaves for food, and its digestive system is uniquely adapted to process their toxins. Aboriginal Australians used eucalyptus for food—lerp insects on branches—wood, and medicines for thousands of years before European settlement.

Eucalyptus was planted worldwide in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries for timber, pulp, and ornament. In some regions including the Mediterranean and California, it has become invasive and alters fire regimes. Fast-growing and efficient at water uptake, it is sometimes planted to drain swamps. But in dry regions, it can deplete groundwater. The stringybark, ironbark, and snow gum are among the most commercially important species.

Eucalyptus survives in poor soil where other trees fail, making it ecologically dominant across Australia's interior. Eucalyptus connects to Australia as the native continent where it evolved and dominates the landscape, to the Australian Outback as the arid interior region where eucalyptus-dominated savanna and woodland thrive, to the koala as an iconic marsupial whose survival depends entirely on eucalyptus leaves, to Aboriginal Australians as peoples who cultivated and used eucalyptus for millennia before colonization, to fire ecology as eucalyptus's evolutionary co-evolution with fire and many species requiring fire to reproduce, and to drought adaptation as a textbook example of morphological and physiological adaptation to water scarcity.
